messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Paramedic
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Workplace: Workplace, Darkness: Dark spaces, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arun had been a paramedic for thirty-five years, a career defined by a steady hand and the ability to impose order on chaos. That sense of control had vanished six months ago on a cold Tuesday night. The call was for an overturned tanker on an industrial access road, far from any streetlights. The scene was plunged into a disorienting darkness, broken only by the strobing red and blue of the emergency lights. As he and his partner approached the wreck, a cloying, sweet smell hit him—a sharp, chemical odour that reminded him instantly and sickeningly of industrial-grade alcohol. Before he could get his respirator properly sealed, he took a deep, reflexive breath. The world dissolved into a searing pain in his lungs and a dizzying wave of nausea. He remembers staggering back, the feeling of choking, and a profound, animal terror that he was dying right there on the asphalt, poisoned from the inside out.

In the weeks that followed his physical recovery, the terror did not recede. It simply hid, waiting. The first time the memory returned in its full force, he was at the station, restocking his rig. He opened a container of alcohol wipes, and the scent, though milder, was enough. Suddenly, he was no longer in the brightly lit ambulance bay but back in the suffocating dark of the crash site, his chest constricting, the same raw fear clawing at his throat. He felt so overwhelmed by the wave of panic that he dropped the box and had to brace himself against the vehicle, gasping for air. He called in sick for the rest of his shift and hasn't been back since. His captain has been patient, but Arun knows that patience is finite.

His home, once a sanctuary, has become a landscape of potential threats. He avoids going into the garage or the basement after dusk; the enclosed dark spaces feel too much like the cab of that overturned truck, trapping him with the memory. His wife, Priya, has noticed how he keeps every light in the house blazing until they go to bed. He cannot bear to be alone, especially not with his own thoughts. The silence is when the rumination begins, an endless, looping film of the accident where he is the failing director, trying to change the scene. If only he’d approached from upwind. If only he’d sealed his mask a second sooner. If only he’d recognised the smell for what it was. To escape this internal critic, Arun insists on constant company. He plans dinners with friends, encourages their adult children to visit multiple times a week, and fills any quiet moment with the television's noise. Priya tries to be understanding, but he can see the exhaustion in her eyes. She misses the quiet evenings they used to share.

The avoidance has bled into every corner of his life, a profound irony for a man who spent his life in medicine. He can’t watch his favourite medical dramas anymore. The sight of an ambulance on the street causes his heart to pound, and he has to look away. A few weeks ago, he needed a routine physical for his life insurance, and the thought of sitting in a doctor’s office, of submitting to any kind of examination, was so intolerable that he cancelled the appointment. It was this act, this turning away from the very concept of care, that crystallised his situation. He was a healer who was terrified of being healed. At sixty-one, he had been looking forward to a proud retirement, celebrating a long career of service. Instead, he feels trapped in a shrinking world, haunted by a single breath on a dark road. He has come to therapy because the man he was—competent, calm, and in control—feels like a stranger, and he is terrified he will never find his way back to him.
